implementation_notes: Go supplies the once semantics twice over. Package-level variable initialisation is performed by the runtime before main, so a value needed by the whole program is simply an eagerly initialised variable or an init() that can fail fast; and sync.Once.Do(f) runs f exactly once with a happens-before edge to every other Do caller that the Go memory model names explicitly, while OnceValue(f), OnceValues(f) and OnceFunc(f) (Go 1.21) wrap the cell so callers receive the value directly. It replaces the whole check-and-lock structure: the guard is the once object, and hand-rolling a double check with sync/atomic buys nothing because Go's cost model is goroutine scheduling, not lock acquisition. A hand-written guard is still justified when initialisation must be per key (a mutex-guarded map, or singleflight for coalescing) or when failures must be retried instead of memoised.
pitfalls: Once memoises failures: a panic inside Do is re-propagated to every caller and an error cached by OnceValues is returned forever, so retry-on-error needs an explicit mutex or a reset protocol.

Do is not reentrant: recursion into the same Once deadlocks, and copying a Once value (passing it by value, or copying a struct that embeds it) breaks the guarantee - go vet flags the copy, but the deadlock is the symptom in production.
OnceValue returns a function whose result must itself be safe for concurrent use: the guard protects initialisation, not a returned map or slice.
Goroutine stack growth and scheduling mean the 'lock-free' claim is irrelevant in Go: measuring the alternative (a mutex around the accessor) usually shows no difference.
